summaries.example: Imagine two friends arguing about whether to join a club. One friend quickly says, “I know exactly what to do!” The other listens, asks what each friend wants, considers possible problems, and gives careful advice. The second friend may show more wisdom—not because they know everything, but because they think carefully, stay open to other views, and try to help everyone live well.
summaries.summary:
Philosophers ask what wisdom really is. Some connect it to virtue, which means having good qualities of character. Socrates is an important example: he examined what people claimed to know and recognized his own limits. This suggests that intellectual humility matters, but simply thinking “I am not wise” cannot be the whole meaning of wisdom. A person can be unsure and still not be wise, while a wise person may sometimes know that they have good understanding.

Other qualities also seem important. Wise people can be courageous, open-minded, imaginative, empathetic, and reflective. They consider different points of view, notice what matters to other people, and think about whether their actions match their values. Philosophers also discuss whether wisdom is mostly about knowing facts, understanding important ideas, or knowing how to make good choices. Many views focus on living well: wisdom should help someone decide what goals matter, how to reach them, and how to deal with problems and limits. There is disagreement about whether wise people must succeed at living well, or whether it is enough that they understand it and are disposed to try. The entry presents these competing views without treating one simple definition as settled.
key_ideas: Socrates is often pictured as wise because he did not pretend to know things he did not know.
Humility alone is not enough for wisdom. A wise person also needs courage, open-mindedness, imagination, empathy, and careful reflection.
Many philosophers think wisdom helps guide other virtues and helps people decide how to live well.
Philosophers disagree about whether a wise person must actually live well, or only understand how to live well and be committed to trying.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about wisdom can help us separate real good judgment from simply sounding clever. It reminds us that making good choices may require listening, self-knowledge, courage, and concern for others—not just having lots of facts. The topic also encourages us to ask how our beliefs and actions fit together when life is difficult.

important_terms.definition: Wisdom is a special kind of human excellence. It involves understanding important matters and using that understanding to make good choices.
A virtue is a good quality of character, such as courage, honesty, kindness, or open-mindedness.
Intellectual humility means recognizing that you may not know everything and being willing to learn.
Practical wisdom means knowing how to choose and act well in real-life situations.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone be wise if they know a lot but never listens to other people?
Is admitting “I do not know” always a sign of wisdom?
What might a wise person do when two good choices seem to conflict?

summaries.example: Suppose two students advise a friend who is deciding whether to leave a demanding activity. Student A knows many facts about scholarships and careers but gives a quick answer without asking about the friend’s health, values, or long-term aims. Student B knows fewer technical details but asks careful questions, considers competing goods, recognizes uncertainty, and explains several possible paths and their costs. The case illustrates why practical wisdom may require more than information: it involves understanding what matters, judging means and consequences, and applying that understanding to a particular life.
summaries.summary:
Contemporary analytic philosophers treat wisdom as a possible form of human excellence and as an epistemic achievement. The entry first examines its relation to virtue. Socrates is presented through Plato’s account in the Apology: he investigates people who claim extensive knowledge and avoids claiming knowledge he lacks. One interpretation, the Socratic Humility Theory, makes wisdom depend on believing that one is not wise. The entry argues that this cannot by itself be sufficient. Some people correctly think they are unwise, and a wise person may reasonably recognize their own wisdom in some contexts. A related proposal focuses on not claiming answers to the deepest philosophical questions, but this too seems both too broad and too demanding.

A fuller picture connects wisdom with several virtues. Intellectual humility, courage, open-mindedness, imagination, empathy, perceptiveness, reflection, and emotional regulation may all contribute. Plato treats wisdom as a guiding virtue, while Aristotle’s practical wisdom helps resolve situations in which different virtues appear to point in different directions. Some philosophers defend the stronger unity of the virtues thesis; others argue that wisdom depends on several virtues without requiring all of them fully.

The entry then asks what the wise person knows or understands. Candidates include justified belief, knowledge, and understanding, with understanding attractive because wisdom involves a flexible grasp of how to live rather than merely receiving advice from others. Many accounts center on living well, but they disagree about whether valuable academic knowledge belongs in wisdom’s domain. key_ideas: Socratic humility is an important starting point, but the claim that wisdom consists in believing one is not wise is too weak: many people have that belief without being wise.
Wisdom is often grounded in a group of intellectual, moral, and social virtues, including humility, courage, open-mindedness, imagination, empathy, reflection, and emotional regulation.
A major dispute concerns the epistemic domain of wisdom. Some views include valuable academic subjects, while others make understanding how to live well the central or exclusive domain.
Practical wisdom requires more than knowing an abstract theory of well-being. It concerns judgment about goals, means, dangers, limits, relationships, and particular circumstances.
Philosophers disagree about whether wisdom requires successful living, coherence between values and actions, or merely a stable commitment or disposition to live well.
The entry distinguishes wisdom from intelligence, cleverness, and specialized skill; being excellent in one narrow field does not automatically make someone wise as a person.
summaries.why_it_matters: The philosophical study of wisdom clarifies a quality often praised but rarely defined. It shows why intelligence, information, confidence, or practical success alone may not be enough. The debate also has implications for education and advice: learning to live well may involve intellectual virtues, reflection, judgment, and the ability to connect general understanding with concrete human problems. Because the theories disagree, the topic invites careful comparison rather than a quick slogan.

important_terms.definition: Wisdom is discussed as both an epistemic good, involving doing well in understanding or belief, and a possible virtue that shapes how a person thinks and acts.
An epistemic good is a way of doing well in inquiry or belief, such as knowing, understanding, or believing appropriately.
Practical wisdom, or phronesis, is the intellectual ability to deliberate well about how to live and what to do in varied circumstances.
A humility theory explains wisdom partly through recognizing one’s limits, especially avoiding claims to know what one does not know.
Reflective discernment is the ability to assess a situation, weigh competing concerns, and adjust one’s life when actions conflict with considered values.
The unity of the virtues thesis says that fully possessing one virtue requires fully possessing the other virtues as well.

questions_to_think_about: Does a person become wiser by learning more facts in an academic subject, if that knowledge does not improve their judgment about life?
Should wisdom require actually living well, or can someone understand how to live well while failing to do so?
How should a wise adviser balance general principles with the details of a particular person’s situation?
Can intellectual humility coexist with confidence in one’s ability to give advice?
Does wisdom require moral goodness, or could a deeply immoral person possess the relevant understanding?

summaries.example: A student hears that a friend wants to quit the school team. One adviser says, “Never quit anything,” while another asks why the friend wants to leave, considers stress and goals, listens to different opinions, and discusses possible choices. The second adviser is closer to the kind of person philosophers may call practically wise. Good advice requires more than a rule or a pile of facts; it requires understanding what matters in this situation and how the choice may affect a life.
summaries.summary:
The entry explores wisdom through two connected questions: what kind of person is wise, and what does that person understand? It begins with virtue, a good quality of character. Socrates is a model because he tests people’s claims to knowledge and recognizes his own limits. This supports a humility-based interpretation of wisdom. However, believing that one is not wise cannot be enough: many people lack confidence without having the deeper excellence associated with wisdom. Also, wise people may sometimes correctly recognize that they know something important.

The discussion therefore widens beyond humility. Courage helps a person examine difficult beliefs and speak honestly. Open-mindedness allows serious attention to other viewpoints. Imagination helps someone see possible solutions, and empathy helps them understand how situations look to others. Reflection lets a person compare their actions with their values and make changes. Plato and Aristotle give wisdom a guiding role among the virtues, although philosophers disagree about whether having one virtue fully requires having all the others.

Wisdom is also described as an epistemic good, meaning a way of doing well in thinking. Theories differ over whether it is mainly justified belief, knowledge, or understanding. Many philosophers agree that wisdom involves living well, but they disagree about what this requires. Some include knowledge in academic fields; others argue that the central subject is how to live. The entry emphasizes that an abstract theory of happiness is not enough. A wise person must understand aims, ways of reaching them, risks, limits, and how to judge different circumstances. key_ideas: Socrates may be wise because he does not pretend to know what he does not know, but philosophers question whether humility alone explains wisdom.
Wisdom appears connected with many virtues, including courage, open-mindedness, imagination, empathy, reflection, and control of one’s reactions.
Some philosophers say wisdom mainly concerns understanding how to live well; others think it also includes doing well in valuable academic subjects.
Practical wisdom is not just knowing a general rule. It involves judging goals, consequences, limits, and the details of a real situation.
There is disagreement about whether a person must live successfully to be wise, or whether understanding and a serious commitment to living well are enough.
Wisdom is different from being clever or highly skilled at one narrow activity.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea of wisdom matters because people often look for guidance when choices are confusing or important. Studying it helps us ask what makes advice reliable: facts, experience, humility, empathy, courage, or the ability to judge a situation. It also shows that philosophy is not only about collecting answers; it can examine the character and understanding needed to use answers well.

important_terms.definition: Wisdom is an important kind of excellence that may involve knowledge, understanding, good character, and guidance about living well.
A virtue is a strong, valuable trait of character that helps someone think, feel, or act well.
Intellectual humility is recognizing the limits of one’s knowledge and avoiding overconfident claims.
Practical wisdom, called phronesis by Aristotle, is good judgment about what to do in changing and difficult situations.
An epistemic good is something valuable in thinking and inquiry, such as knowledge, understanding, or well-supported belief.
Open-mindedness is the virtue of seriously considering reasonable alternative ideas or perspectives.

questions_to_think_about: Why might simply saying “I am not wise” fail to make someone wise?
Can a person be wise without knowing much about modern science or technology?
When two good qualities, such as courage and caution, seem to disagree, what could wisdom contribute?
Should a person who gives wise advice also follow that advice?
What is the difference between being clever at a task and being wise about life?
